tagline: Four island states across the Pacific
overview:
The Federated States of Micronesia is a country of more than 600 islands spread across a stretch of the western Pacific about 2,700 kilometers wide, though all its land together comes to only about 702 km², a little smaller than New York City. It is organized into four states, Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae, each with its own languages and traditions. The capital, Palikir, sits on the island of Pohnpei.

About 110,000 people live in Micronesia. English is the official language and serves as the common tongue between the states, while Chuukese, Pohnpeian, Yapese, Kosraean and several other languages are spoken at home. The country is a republic in free association with the United States, which handles defense and provides financial support, and Micronesians may live and work in the US. Fishing licenses, farming and aid support the economy, and rising seas and stronger typhoons threaten the lowest islands.
landAndNature: The islands come in two kinds: high volcanic islands such as Pohnpei and Kosrae, steep and green with rainforest and waterfalls, and low coral atolls barely above the waves. Pohnpei is one of the rainiest places on Earth, with some inland spots receiving more than 7,000 millimeters of rain a year. Mangroves fringe the shores, and the reefs are among the richest in the Pacific, with manta rays gathering at cleaning stations off Yap and sharks patrolling the drop-offs. Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of ships sunk during World War II, now coral gardens. Coconut crabs, the largest land crabs anywhere, climb the palms.
peopleAndCulture: Each state keeps its own customs. On Yap, huge stone discs called rai, some over three meters across, are still recognized as traditional money, and ownership passes by agreement without the stones ever being moved. On Pohnpei, ceremonies center on sakau, a drink pressed from a pepper plant root. Breadfruit, taro, yams, bananas, fish and coconut are staple foods, often baked in earth ovens. Sailing canoes and traditional navigation are being taught again to younger generations. Clan ties and respect for elders shape village life, most people are Christian, and baseball and basketball are played everywhere.
history: Voyagers settled these islands thousands of years ago, and on Pohnpei they built Nan Madol, a city of nearly a hundred artificial islets made from huge basalt logs stacked in the shallows between about 1200 and 1600, the only ancient city of its kind built on a coral reef. Spain claimed the islands, sold them to Germany in 1899, and Japan took them during World War I and later fortified them. Heavy fighting reached Chuuk in 1944. After the war the islands were administered by the United States under a United Nations trusteeship. The Federated States of Micronesia adopted a constitution in 1979 and became fully independent in 1986.
funFacts: On Yap, stone discs up to three meters wide still count as money, and owners change without the stones moving.
Nan Madol, built from stacked basalt logs on a reef, is the only ancient city of its kind in the Pacific.
Micronesia's islands are scattered over roughly three million square kilometers of ocean, though its land is tiny.
Chuuk Lagoon holds dozens of ships sunk in 1944, now covered in coral and explored by divers.
Coconut crabs in Micronesia can weigh over four kilograms and crack open coconuts with their claws.
